newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean panel proposes sweeping financial reforms.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean panel proposes sweeping financial reforms.

text.p: In a presentation to South Korean President Kim Young-sam on Wednesday a panel studying financial reforms recommended sharply increasing central bank independence and the bank's control over monetary policy.
In comments released earlier Kim said he would support the panel's recommended reforms.

The Presidential Commission for Financial Reform said its reform proposals were aimed at improving international competitiveness, establishing a user-oriented financial industry and building healthy financial institutions.
The 31-member commission, composed of bankers, business leaders and scholars, generally suggested giving more management autonomy to financial institutions and lifting various government regulations.
Much of the central bank's new authority under the commission's proposals would come at the expense of the Ministry of Finance and Economy..
The commission proposed unifying the three financial watchdogs -- the Office of Bank Supervision, the Securities Supervisory Board and the Insurance Supervisory Board.
It said the unified financial supervisory board should be under the direct control of the Prime Minister and that the head of the new board should have ministerial rank.
At present, heads of the supervisory agencies report to the finance minister. Analysts said the commission's plan was aimed at limiting the Finance Ministry's functions to policy-making.

The commission said central bank autonomy was needed to stabilise prices because controlling inflation could conflict with government efforts to promote economic growth. The panel said the central bank should be given full authority to design and implement monetary and inflation policies.

The panel said the Monetary Board, which currently sets monetary policies, should be the highest decision-making body under the central bank. It recommended the central bank governor chair the Monetary Board.
The finance minister now heads the board and recommends to the president five of nine board members.
The commission proposed a seven-member board, consisting of central bank officials and business and financial industry representatives. It excluded Finance Ministry officials from the board.

After much discussion the commission finally decided to uphold the current four percent individual shareholding limit in South Korean banks. However, it said the ceiling could be raised to 10 percent under certain conditions and with prior government approval.
The finance ministry will review the proposals and submit implementing legislation to a special session of the National Assembly in June.
The commission also proposed introducing financial holding companies. A holding company has control of one or more other companies, often through share ownership.
Such companies would be allowed to own wholly-owned banks or non-banking financial institutions such as their subsidiaries but not non-financial industry companies.

The panel also said companies with bank credits exceeding 500 billion won should report consolidated financial statements, which would include a balance sheet, profit and loss statement and cash-flow statement. The consolidated statement should be inspected by external auditors. -- Seoul newsroom 822 727-5647
